title: Legs that "just don't feel right" in a 28-year-old accountant
desc: This station involves a focused history and a lower limb neurological examination of a 28-year-old accountant in the ED. For 4 days she has had numbness and tingling spreading up her legs, and her legs are getting weaker. She also has urinary retention. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, blood results and an MRI of the whole spine and brain. They place the lesion in the thoracic spinal cord, exclude cord compression, recognise an inflammatory demyelinating myelitis, and manage it in the ED with neurology. They then answer her questions about walking again and multiple sclerosis.
focus: Lower limb neurological examination: separating upper from lower motor neuron signs, finding a sensory level, and treating a new myelopathy as an emergency until cord compression is excluded
diagnosis: Acute transverse myelitis (lesion at T7-T8 vertebral level, T10 sensory level)
Second demyelinating event after probable right optic neuritis 2 years ago: likely relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (first presentation to medical care)
stem: You are the junior medical officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Katie Johnson, a 28-year-old accountant, came in by ambulance this morning because her "legs just don't feel right". She is lying on a trolley in a cubicle, wearing shorts and a hospital gown. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Katie and perform a focused lower limb neurological examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think she needs as you go (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Katie's observations, blood results and MRI report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Katie Johnson, 28, an accountant. You are lying on the trolley in shorts. You are alert, articulate and comfortable at rest, but frightened that your legs are not working. Answer clearly. Give the history below only when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining. When asked to move your legs, move them slowly and weakly. Your right foot barely moves. Your left foot moves a little better.

Opening line: "My legs just don't feel right. They've been going numb and weak for a few days and now I can't even stand up."

The legs (give only when asked)

  • Onset: it started 4 days ago with pins and needles in both feet, both at the same time.
  • Spread: over the next 2 days the tingling and numbness crept up both legs. It now reaches "about my belly button". Below that, things feel "dead and fuzzy", and bath water did not feel hot.
  • Weakness: 2 days ago your legs felt heavy and stiff and you kept tripping. Yesterday you had to hold on to the walls. This morning you could not stand, and your partner called the ambulance.
  • Balance: you have been unsteady and could not tell where your feet were without looking at them.
  • Band: a tight feeling around your waist, "like a belt done up too tight", for 3 days. There is a dull ache in the middle of your back, 2/10.
  • Your right leg is weaker and stiffer than the left. The numbness feels a bit worse on the left.

Bladder, bowels and saddle (give only when asked)

  • You have not been able to pass urine since last night, even though you felt you needed to. A nurse put a catheter in when you arrived. "They said there was nearly a litre in there."
  • Your bowels have not opened for 2 days. You have not had any accidents.
  • Tingling around your bottom, and you could not feel the toilet paper properly yesterday.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No fall, injury, accident or heavy lifting. No recent back injections or operations.
  • No fever, sweats or shivers. No weight loss. No cancer, now or in the past.
  • No blood thinners and no bleeding problems. You have never injected drugs.
  • No severe back pain, just the dull ache.
  • Your arms and hands feel normal. No neck pain. No electric shocks down your back when you bend your neck.
  • No problems with your face, speech, swallowing or breathing. No headache. Your vision is fine at the moment and you have no double vision.

Previous episodes (only if asked about any previous neurological or eye problems)

  • About 2 years ago your right eye went blurry. Colours looked "washed out" and it hurt to move the eye. It got better by itself over about 6 weeks.
  • An optometrist said it was "probably some inflammation" and told you to see your GP if it happened again. You never followed it up.
  • No other episodes of numbness, weakness or unsteadiness that you can remember.

Recent illness

  • A cold about 3 weeks ago, which got better within a week. No diarrhoea. No recent travel. No recent vaccinations.

Past medical history

  • Otherwise well. No operations.
  • If asked: your last period was 2 weeks ago and you do not think you could be pregnant.

Medications and allergies

  • The combined oral contraceptive pill. Nothing else, no supplements.
  • No allergies.

Family history

  • Your mother has an underactive thyroid. Nothing else you know of.

Social history

  • Accountant. You have a big audit deadline next week.
  • You live with your partner, Tom, in a second-floor flat with no lift. You were fully independent until 4 days ago. You drive.
  • Never smoked. About 4 standard drinks on weekends. No recreational drugs. You go to the gym twice a week.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "I thought I'd pinched a nerve at the gym."
  • Concerns: "Is it a stroke? Am I going to be able to walk again?"
  • Expectations: you want to know what is going on and what is going to happen today.
  • Question to ask: "Could this be something like MS? My friend's mum has it."

During the station

  • If the candidate asks you to stand or walk, try to sit forward and say: "I can't, my legs just won't hold me." The nurse steps in to stop you falling.

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • Gives the observations and a bedside glucose when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If asked about the catheter: "It went in at triage at 09:20 and drained 950 mL of clear urine."
  • If asked about pregnancy testing, or when an MRI with contrast is ordered: "A urine pregnancy test was done at triage: negative."
  • If the candidate orders an MRI, bloods, a senior review or a referral, says "I'll get that organised." If an MRI is requested: "Radiology can take her at 11:00." If a drug is ordered without a dose or route, asks "What dose and route would you like?"
  • If the candidate orders corticosteroids before any imaging, asks once: "Do you want those before or after the MRI?" Let the candidate answer.
  • If the candidate asks for blood or MRI results, says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General inspection: lying comfortably on the trolley, alert, appears well. Weight 65 kg. No walking aids. A urinary catheter is in place, draining clear urine. No distress, tremor, chorea, myoclonus or other abnormal movements.
  • Observations: RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 118/74, HR 76 regular, temperature 36.8 °C, pain 2/10 (dull mid-back ache and waist band), CRT 2 seconds. Bedside glucose 5.4 mmol/L.
  • Local inspection: no wasting, joint deformity, swelling, scars or skin changes. No fasciculations, including after tapping the muscles.
  • Gait: unable to stand or walk. Heel-to-toe, walking on heels and toes, Romberg's test, squat, Trendelenburg and the pull test cannot be done.
  • Tone: increased, spastic tone in both legs, more on the right (a catch on quick knee flexion). No clonus at the ankles or knees.
  • Power (MRC), pyramidal pattern (flexors weaker than extensors), right worse:
    • Right: hip flexion 3/5, hip extension 4/5, hip abduction 3/5, hip adduction 4/5; knee flexion 3/5, knee extension 4-/5; ankle dorsiflexion 2/5, plantarflexion 3/5, inversion and eversion 2/5.
    • Left (generally one grade better): hip flexion 4/5, hip extension 5/5, hip abduction 4/5, hip adduction 5/5; knee flexion 4/5, knee extension 4+/5; ankle dorsiflexion 3/5, plantarflexion 4/5, inversion and eversion 3/5.
  • Reflexes: brisk knee and ankle jerks on both sides. Plantars upgoing (extensor) on both sides.
  • Coordination: heel-shin, toe-finger and foot tapping are slow but accurate, in keeping with the weakness.
  • Sensation: loss is worst in the dorsal columns. Proprioception is absent at both great toes and ankles. Vibration (128 Hz fork) is absent at the toes and ankles and reduced at the knees on both sides. Pinprick, temperature and light touch are reduced (not absent) in all lower limb dermatomes and up the trunk to the umbilicus, more on the left, and normal above it: a sensory level at T10.
  • Perianal sensation and anal tone (if the candidate says they would examine them): reduced perianal sensation with tingling; on PR, normal resting anal tone but reduced voluntary anal squeeze.
  • Spine (if examined): no deformity, no step and no tenderness.
  • Abdomen (if examined): soft and non-tender. Bladder not palpable with the catheter in.
  • Upper limbs (if the candidate says they would complete with them): tone, power (5/5), reflexes, coordination and sensation normal and symmetrical.
  • Cranial nerves (if the candidate says they would complete with them): visual acuity 6/6 in each eye, no relative afferent pupillary defect, eye movements full with no nystagmus, other cranial nerves normal. Fundoscopy: mild temporal pallor of the right optic disc; left disc normal.
  • Urine pregnancy test (done at triage): negative.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Katie's identity and gains consent. Exposes the legs with dignity and positions her lying supine so both legs can be seen.
Acknowledges her fear about walking and her worry about stroke and MS, uses plain language, and answers honestly without false reassurance.
History
Characterises the onset and progression:

kids.x: Tingling began in both feet 4 days ago and has ascended to the level of the umbilicus
Progressive leg heaviness, stiffness and weakness (right worse), from tripping to unable to stand this morning
Band-like tightness around the waist, and unsteadiness without looking at her feet

check.x: Asks about bladder, bowel and saddle symptoms and elicits: urinary retention since last night (catheterised with about 950 mL), bowels not open for 2 days, and perianal tingling.

Screens for a compressive, infective or traumatic cause in at least four of: trauma or lifting, fever, cancer or weight loss, anticoagulants or bleeding, injecting drug use, severe back pain, and recent spinal procedures.
Screens for symptoms above the lesion, including at least arm symptoms, breathing and vision, plus any two of neck pain or Lhermitte's, face, speech and swallowing (all normal).
Asks about previous neurological or visual episodes and elicits the painful, blurred right eye with washed-out colours 2 years ago that recovered over about 6 weeks.
Asks about recent infection (a cold 3 weeks ago) and about pregnancy and contraception (last period 2 weeks ago, on the combined pill).
Takes the past history, medications and allergies:

kids.x: Otherwise well; combined oral contraceptive pill only

check.x: Takes a social and functional history: accountant, lives with her partner in a second-floor flat with no lift, independent until 4 days ago, drives, non-smoker, alcohol on weekends.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thought it was a pinched nerve, fears a stroke and not walking again, asks about MS.
Examination

Performs general and local inspection. Notes the urinary catheter draining clear urine, no aids, no abnormal movements, and no wasting or fasciculations (looks for fasciculations and tries to elicit them).
Asks to assess gait and stays close to prevent a fall. Notes she cannot stand, so heel-to-toe, heels, toes, Romberg's test and squat cannot be done.
Assesses tone and tests for ankle and knee clonus. Finds increased spastic tone in both legs (more on the right) and no clonus.

Tests power at the hip, knee and ankle, comparing sides, and reports it on the MRC scale: pyramidal-pattern weakness, right worse, with hip flexion, knee flexion and ankle dorsiflexion weaker than the extensors (right hip flexion 3/5, hip extension 4/5, knee flexion 3/5, knee extension 4-/5, ankle dorsiflexion 2/5, plantarflexion 3/5; left generally one grade better).
check.d: Credit the pattern (flexors weaker than extensors, right worse) without requiring every grade.

check.x: Tests knee and ankle reflexes and plantar responses and reports them in correct terms: brisk knee and ankle jerks and upgoing plantars on both sides.
Tests coordination (heel-shin, toe-finger or foot tapping) and interprets the slow but accurate result in light of the weakness.
Examines sensation systematically:

kids.x: Tests at least one spinothalamic modality (pinprick or temperature) and one dorsal column modality (vibration or proprioception), with eyes closed, by dermatome, comparing sides and against a normal reference point
Moves up from the feet onto the trunk and finds a sensory level at the umbilicus (T10)
Finds dorsal-column-predominant loss: absent proprioception at the great toes and ankles and vibration absent at the toes and ankles, with pinprick reduced (not absent) and worse on the left

check.x: Says they would examine perianal sensation and anal tone, and finds reduced perianal sensation, normal resting anal tone and reduced voluntary anal squeeze.
States they would complete with an upper limb and cranial nerve examination (normal, apart from right optic disc pallor if fundoscopy is done), spinal palpation and a full set of observations.
Interpretation

Localises the lesion: upper motor neuron signs (spastic tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, no wasting or fasciculations) with a T10 sensory level and sphincter involvement, and normal arms and cranial nerves, place it in the thoracic spinal cord at about the T10 cord segment. States that cauda equina syndrome would give lower motor neuron signs.
check.d: Earned from the justification in the answer to question 2.

check.x: Interprets the observations: all vital signs in the white (normal) zone and afebrile, but nurse concern and a sensory level rising from T10 to T8 at 13:10 show a progressing myelopathy that the vital signs do not reflect; staff concern alone meets local escalation (Clinical Review) criteria.
check.d: Naming the specific chart criterion is not required.

check.x: Interprets the bloods: normal white cell count and CRP argue against infection such as an epidural abscess; normal B12, glucose and renal function; normal coagulation (safe for LP); β-hCG negative. They are the baseline before steroids.
Interprets the MRI:

kids.x: No cord compression, mass, disc, collection or haematoma, so this is a neurology rather than a neurosurgical problem

A short-segment, peripheral (less than half the cross-section), enhancing intramedullary T2 lesion at T7-T8 (vertebral level) with mild cord swelling, which corresponds to the T10 cord segment found on examination: an inflammatory myelitis
Non-enhancing periventricular and juxtacortical brain lesions typical of demyelination, which point to multiple sclerosis (supported by the earlier eye episode if it was elicited)

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as acute (partial) transverse myelitis (lesion at T7-T8 vertebral level, T10 sensory level) with likely relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with its supporting features.
check.d: Credit acute (partial) transverse myelitis with likely relapsing-remitting MS, justified by the MRI (cord plus periventricular/juxtacortical lesions) with or without the earlier eye episode. Credit "second attack" wording only as an extra if the eye history was elicited. Do not credit a diagnosis of idiopathic transverse myelitis alone or cord compression.

check.x: Names at least three differentials, each with a feature against it, from: spinal cord compression (tumour, abscess, disc, haematoma), idiopathic or post-infectious transverse myelitis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, traumatic cord injury and cauda equina syndrome.
Management
In Part 1, recognises a new spastic paraparesis with a sensory level and sphincter involvement as an emergency. Asks for senior ED review and an urgent MRI of the whole spine.
check.d: Credit only if the candidate states or orders this during Part 1 (to the nurse or the examiner). Not earned in Part 2.

check.x: Escalates the rising sensory level now: senior ED doctor to the bedside and urgent neurology review in the ED.

Treats the myelitis on neurology advice, now that MRI has excluded compression and the bloods show no infection: high-dose methylprednisolone (typically 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days), with glucose monitoring. Plasma exchange is an option if she does not respond.

Completes the work-up as directed by neurology: lumbar puncture (cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands with a paired serum sample, and infection screen), ideally before the first methylprednisolone dose if this does not delay treatment, and serum aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies.
Orders supportive care:

kids.x: Catheter care and a bowel regimen for the neurogenic bladder and bowel
VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis (immobile, on the combined pill), timed around the lumbar puncture.
kids.d: Withholding the combined pill with alternative contraception advice is good practice but not needed for this box.

kids.x: Pressure area care, falls precautions, physiotherapy and occupational therapy

check.x: Admits her under neurology, with regular neurological observations of the sensory level, power, arm strength and breathing.

Explains to Katie in plain words: inflammation in the spinal cord, not a stroke and not pressure on the cord; MS is likely (brain lesions plus the earlier eye episode), and neurology will confirm it with an LP and blood tests; effective treatments exist. Is honest that recovery is often good but cannot be promised.
Safety netting

Sets escalation triggers for the nurses: the numbness rising further, weakness or numbness spreading to the arms, any difficulty breathing or a weak cough, new fever or severe back pain, and catheter problems.

Tells Katie in plain words what needs urgent help: numbness creeping higher, arms becoming weak or numb, or trouble breathing (tell a nurse now; call 000 after discharge). New loss of vision, or new weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel problems lasting more than a day, need prompt review by neurology or the ED.
Arranges follow-up, at least two of: neurology clinic/MS nurse, rehabilitation, GP review, work certificate; plus no driving until neurology clears her (required).

part2.lead: It is now 13:15. Katie had her MRI at 11:00, after your assessment. Here are her observations since you saw her, her blood results and the MRI report.
part2.patient:
For the fourth question, Katie is frightened but calm. As the candidate explains, ask once, if it has not already been covered:

  • "Do I need an operation?"

If the candidate uses jargon (myelitis, demyelination, lesion), ask "What does that mean?" If the candidate is honest that MS is likely, say quietly: "Okay. I'd rather know."

handover.label: Observations since your assessment
handover.result: Room air throughout. Urinary catheter in situ since 09:20 (950 mL residual), draining clear urine. Sensory level checked by the nurse with a neurotip at each set.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 16 to 18, SpO2 98 to 99% on room air, BP 116 to 120 systolic, HR 76 to 84 regular, temperature 36.8 to 36.9 °C, alert, pain 2 to 3/10. Every value is in the white zone at all three times. At 10:40 and 12:15 the sensory level is T10. At 13:10 the nurse is concerned: the numbness has risen to just below the ribs (T8).
  • Meaning: the myelopathy is progressing over hours, and the vital signs do not show it. She is afebrile, which argues against an epidural abscess. The level has risen to T8, now above the lesion imaged at 11:00, so the inflammation is extending. This is still below T6 (the level linked to autonomic dysreflexia and neurogenic shock) and spares the diaphragm, but abdominal and lower intercostal weakness can weaken her cough, and a level still rising towards the cervical cord would threaten breathing.
  • Changes: no value triggers a clinical review or rapid response. Staff concern is itself a Clinical Review criterion, so she needs immediate medical review: senior ED doctor now, neurology in the ED, and re-examination of the level, arms, cough and breathing. Call a rapid response if breathing is affected or any value reaches the red zone. Treatment should not wait.

rows.note: Sensory level T10. Catheter draining clear urine
Back from MRI. Sensory level T10
Says numbness has crept up to just below her ribs. Pinprick level now T8. Arms feel normal. Doctor informed

handover.label: Blood results
handover.model:
• Read: Hb, white cell count, neutrophils and platelets are normal. CRP 2 is normal. Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine (eGFR above 90) and glucose 5.4 are normal. B12 410 is normal. INR and APTT are normal. β-hCG below 5: not pregnant.
  • Meaning: no sign of infection or systemic inflammation, which with the absence of fever makes an epidural abscess unlikely. A normal B12 makes subacute combined degeneration unlikely. Normal coagulation makes a spontaneous epidural haematoma unlikely.
  • Changes: Normal platelets and coagulation mean a lumbar puncture is safe. The negative serum β-hCG confirms the triage urine test, which was negative before gadolinium. The glucose is the baseline for steroid monitoring.

handover.label: MRI whole spine and brain report
handover.result:
Examination: MRI whole spine (cervical, thoracic and lumbar) and MRI brain, before and after IV gadolinium. Sagittal and axial T2, STIR and post-contrast T1; brain FLAIR. 11:00.

Clinical details: 28-year-old woman. 4 days of ascending sensory disturbance, spastic paraparesis with pyramidal-pattern weakness, right worse, sensory level T10, urinary retention and reduced voluntary anal squeeze. ?Cord compression ?myelitis.

Findings:

  • Thoracic cord: a focal T2 and STIR hyperintense intramedullary lesion at the T7-T8 vertebral level, about 1.5 vertebral segments long, eccentric and dorsolateral on the right, occupying less than half of the cord cross-sectional area, with mild cord swelling and patchy gadolinium enhancement.
  • Cervical cord and conus: normal signal. The conus ends at L1. The cauda equina roots are normal and do not enhance.
  • Spinal canal: no extradural or intradural mass, collection or haematoma. No disc protrusion compressing the cord or cauda equina. No cord compression at any level.
  • Vertebrae and soft tissues: normal alignment and marrow signal. No fracture or destructive lesion. Paraspinal soft tissues normal.
  • Brain: three ovoid T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular white matter, oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles, and one juxtacortical lesion in the left frontal lobe. None enhance. No infratentorial lesion. No mass, haemorrhage or hydrocephalus. The optic nerves show no acute abnormality.

Conclusion: a short-segment, peripheral, enhancing myelitis at T7-T8 with no compressive lesion. Non-enhancing cerebral white matter lesions in a distribution typical of demyelination. Together, these favour an inflammatory demyelinating process such as multiple sclerosis. The short, peripheral cord lesion occupying less than half the cross-section is less typical of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Correlate with CSF and serum aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies.
handover.model:
• Read: the scan covers the whole spine and the brain with contrast. There is a short (about 1.5 segments), peripheral (less than half the cross-section), swollen, enhancing intramedullary lesion at the T7-T8 vertebral level. Nothing compresses the cord at any level: no disc, mass, abscess or haematoma. The vertebrae are normal and the cauda equina is normal. In the brain there are non-enhancing periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles and a juxtacortical lesion.
  • Meaning: the lesion at the T7-T8 vertebrae overlies about the T10-T11 cord segments, so it fits the T10 sensory level (the sensory level is at or below the lesion); in the lower thoracic spine, cord segments lie about three vertebrae above the vertebra of the same number. Its right dorsolateral position fits the right-sided weakness and dorsal column loss. The cause is inflammatory, not compressive. Enhancing and non-enhancing lesions together, in the spinal cord and periventricular and juxtacortical areas, show demyelination in different places at different times. With the earlier painful right visual loss (likely optic neuritis) and the pale right disc, this is a second attack and points to multiple sclerosis. A short, peripheral lesion makes NMOSD less likely but does not exclude it.
  • Changes: no neurosurgical lesion, so this is managed by neurology: high-dose methylprednisolone, LP with oligoclonal bands, and aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies. Neurology confirms the diagnosis.

ask: You are now calling the neurology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Katie Johnson, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer, including where you think the lesion is.
Outline your management of Katie now, here in the emergency department, including what you want the nurses to escalate to you.
Katie asks you, "Will I walk again, and is it MS?" Please answer her, including what she should watch out for and the follow-up she will need.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED JMO; Katie Johnson, 28.
  • Situation: acute thoracic myelopathy; MRI shows an enhancing myelitis at T7-T8 (vertebral level) with no compression; sensory level rising.
  • Background: 4 days of ascending numbness, progressive leg weakness, urinary retention (950 mL), constipation, perianal tingling; painful right visual blurring 2 years ago that resolved; cold 3 weeks ago; combined pill; no allergies.
  • Assessment: spastic paraparesis R>L with UMN signs, dorsal-column-predominant loss, T10 level, reduced voluntary squeeze. Obs all white zone and afebrile, but nurse concerned at 13:10 with the level rising T10 to T8; arms normal. Bloods normal (CRP 2, coags normal, hCG negative). MRI: enhancing cord lesion, no compression, brain lesions typical of demyelination.
  • Recommendation: please review in ED now; IV methylprednisolone advice; LP and AQP4/MOG antibodies; admit under neurology.

Acute transverse myelitis (lesion at T7-T8 vertebral level, T10 sensory level), a second demyelinating event after probable right optic neuritis 2 years ago: likely relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (first presentation to medical care). UMN signs, T10 level, sphincters and normal arms place the lesion in the thoracic cord. MRI: short, peripheral, enhancing cord lesion with typical brain lesions. Pale right disc. (If the eye episode was not elicited, likely MS justified by the cord plus brain lesions earns the mark.)

  • Cord compression (tumour, abscess, disc, haematoma): for: paraparesis, level, sphincters; against: no trauma, fever, cancer or anticoagulants, normal CRP, no compression on MRI.
  • Idiopathic or post-infectious transverse myelitis: for: cold 3 weeks ago; against: brain lesions, previous eye episode.
  • NMOSD: for: myelitis plus previous optic neuritis; against: short peripheral lesion, MS-type brain lesions; AQP4 pending.
  • Trauma: against: no injury, normal vertebrae.
  • Cauda equina syndrome: against: UMN signs and a truncal level.

1. Senior ED doctor to the bedside now for the rising level; urgent neurology review in ED. Re-examine the level, arms, cough and breathing; rapid response if breathing is affected.
  2. Compression and infection excluded (MRI, afebrile, normal CRP and WCC): high-dose methylprednisolone, typically 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days, on neurology advice; glucose monitoring. Plasma exchange if no response (specialist).
  3. LP (cells, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands with paired serum, infection screen), ideally before the first methylprednisolone dose if this does not delay treatment, and serum AQP4 and MOG antibodies.
  4. Supportive: catheter, bowels, VTE prophylaxis after LP (consider withholding the combined pill), pressure care, physio/OT; admit neurology with neuro obs.
  5. Nurse triggers: level rising, arm weakness or numbness, breathing difficulty or weak cough, fever or severe back pain, catheter problems.

• What it is: inflammation in the spinal cord, which stops messages getting through to the legs and bladder. It is not a stroke, nothing is pressing on the cord, and no operation is needed.
  • MS: honestly, the spots on the brain scan and the eye episode make MS likely; neurology will confirm with a lumbar puncture and blood tests; effective treatments exist.
  • Walking: many people improve over weeks to months with steroids and rehabilitation, but full recovery cannot be promised.
  • Watch for: numbness creeping higher, weak or numb arms, trouble breathing: tell a nurse now, and call 000 after discharge. New vision loss, weakness or bladder problems lasting more than a day: neurology or the ED.
  • Follow-up: neurology clinic and MS nurse, rehabilitation, GP, work certificate, no driving until neurology clears her.

ddx.dx: Acute transverse myelitis (lesion at T7-T8 vertebral level, T10 sensory level), a second demyelinating event after probable right optic neuritis 2 years ago: likely relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (first presentation to medical care)
ddx.for: A 28-year-old woman with a 4-day asymmetric spastic paraparesis, a T10 sensory level, sphincter involvement, a probable optic neuritis 2 years ago with right disc pallor, a short, peripheral, enhancing cord lesion at T7-T8, and non-enhancing periventricular and juxtacortical brain lesions.
ddx.against: Neurology still needs to confirm the diagnosis (CSF oligoclonal bands, negative AQP4 and MOG antibodies).

ddx.dx: Spinal cord compression (tumour, epidural abscess, disc prolapse or epidural haematoma)
ddx.for: She has a new paraparesis with a sensory level, urinary retention and reduced voluntary anal squeeze.
ddx.against: She has no trauma, fever, cancer, anticoagulants or severe back pain, her CRP and white cell count are normal, and MRI shows no compression at any level.

ddx.for: She is a young woman with a myelitis and an earlier probable optic neuritis.
ddx.against: The cord lesion is short (about 1.5 segments, not 3 or more), peripheral and less than half the cross-section, and the brain lesions are typical of MS; aquaporin-4 antibodies are pending.

ddx.dx: Idiopathic or post-infectious acute transverse myelitis
ddx.for: She had a cold 3 weeks ago and has an inflammatory cord lesion that evolved over days.
ddx.against: Her brain lesions and earlier eye episode point to a relapsing demyelinating disease rather than a single post-infectious event.

ddx.for: She goes to the gym twice a week.
ddx.against: She has had no injury or heavy lifting, no spinal tenderness, and normal vertebrae on MRI.

ddx.for: She has urinary retention, perianal sensory loss and reduced voluntary anal squeeze.
ddx.against: She has upper motor neuron signs (spastic tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars) and a truncal sensory level, and the cauda equina is normal on MRI.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and glucose when asked. Give each block of the Exam findings as soon as the candidate names the component and shows or describes the technique; do not wait for every movement to be tested in full. Katie cannot stand, so give the gait finding when the candidate asks her to walk, and credit the candidate for staying close. Give the upper limb and cranial nerve findings only if the candidate says they would complete the examination with them. Give perianal sensation and anal tone when the candidate says they would examine them. Expect about 3 to 4 minutes of history and 6 to 7 minutes of examination. If the candidate asks for an MRI or senior review in Part 1, the nurse confirms; credit item 32. If blood or MRI results are requested, say they come in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. Credit localisation (item 25) from the justification in the answer to question 2. For the fourth question, the person playing Katie asks the questions in the Part 2 script.

A high-performing candidate takes a short, targeted history: the ascending pattern, the bladder, bowel and saddle symptoms, the red flags for compression, symptoms above the lesion, and the earlier eye episode. They examine in a logical order (inspection, gait, tone, power, reflexes, coordination, sensation), use correct terms, and map a sensory level up onto the trunk. They decide early that this is an upper motor neuron picture, ask for perianal sensation and anal tone, and request an urgent MRI of the whole spine before the end of Part 1. In Part 2 they see that a rising level outweighs a white zone chart, confirm from the MRI that there is no compression, recognise a demyelinating myelitis as a second attack, and plan steroids, LP and antibodies with neurology.

A borderline candidate tests power and reflexes without a structure, stops sensory testing at the legs and misses the level, or forgets the sphincters. They may call the picture cauda equina syndrome, treat it as a non-urgent outpatient problem, start steroids before compression has been excluded without a reason, or miss the change in the sensory level.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute transverse myelitis (lesion at T7-T8 vertebral level, T10 sensory level), a second demyelinating event after probable right optic neuritis 2 years ago: likely relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (first presentation to medical care)

Katie has a myelopathy: an acute spinal cord syndrome. The examination shows this in two steps.

  1. Upper or lower motor neuron? Increased spastic tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, weakness in a pyramidal pattern (hip flexion, knee flexion and ankle dorsiflexion weaker than the extensors), and no wasting or fasciculations are upper motor neuron signs. A lower motor neuron lesion (roots, cauda equina, peripheral nerve) gives reduced tone, wasting, fasciculations, absent reflexes and downgoing plantars.
  2. Where? Both legs are affected (right more than left) and the arms and cranial nerves are normal, so the lesion is below the cervical cord. A sensory level at the umbilicus (T10), with bladder, bowel and perianal involvement, places it in the thoracic cord at or above the T10 cord segment, which lies at about the T7-T8 vertebrae. A cortical lesion would not give a truncal sensory level, and a cerebellar lesion would not cause weakness with upgoing plantars.

The pattern is partial: the right leg is weaker, dorsal column loss is worst, and pinprick is reduced (not absent) and worse on the left. This fits an eccentric right dorsolateral lesion. A partial, asymmetric myelitis from a short, peripheral lesion is the pattern typical of MS. A complete, symmetric myelitis from a long, central lesion is more typical of NMOSD or idiopathic transverse myelitis.

Reduced voluntary anal squeeze in an acute cord lesion reflects disrupted sacral pathways. Resting tone is normal here, and the finding does not on its own mean the lesion is in the cauda equina. Cauda equina syndrome gives lower motor neuron signs and saddle anaesthesia without a truncal level, so it does not fit these findings.

Her history points to demyelination. Symptoms evolved over days in a young woman, with a band-like truncal sensation (common in myelitis). Two years ago she had an episode of painful, blurred vision with washed-out colours that recovered over weeks. That is the classic story of optic neuritis, and the pale temporal disc is objective support. This myelitis is therefore a second clinical attack, not a clinically isolated syndrome. The MRI shows a short, enhancing cord lesion (new) and non-enhancing periventricular and juxtacortical brain lesions (older). These lesions are in more than one typical site (dissemination in space; the 2024 McDonald revision adds the optic nerve as a fifth site). Enhancing and non-enhancing lesions together also show lesions of different ages (dissemination in time). The 2024 revision no longer requires this, but it adds support. With two clinical attacks with objective evidence (the pale right disc and the current cord signs) plus MRI dissemination in space, she meets the criteria for MS once mimics such as NMOSD and MOG antibody disease are excluded. Neurology makes the final diagnosis, often supported by CSF oligoclonal bands.

Differentials that matter

  • Spinal cord compression (metastasis or primary tumour, epidural abscess, disc prolapse, epidural haematoma): the must-not-miss diagnosis, because decompression is time-critical. Red flags are trauma, cancer, fever or injecting drug use, anticoagulants, and severe or night back pain. None is present here, and the MRI excludes compression.
  • Idiopathic or post-infectious transverse myelitis: may follow a viral illness. Katie's brain lesions and earlier optic neuritis make a relapsing disease more likely.
  • Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder: also causes myelitis and optic neuritis, but usually with a longitudinally extensive, central cord lesion (3 or more vertebral segments) and aquaporin-4 antibodies. Separating it from MS matters because some MS treatments can worsen NMOSD. MOG antibody disease is a further mimic.
  • Trauma: excluded by the history and normal vertebrae.
  • Others worth knowing: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration, dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts), spinal cord infarction (sudden onset, often with back pain), infection (HIV, syphilis, HTLV-1), and, rarely, amyloidosis.

The lower limb neurological examination

Prepare a tendon hammer, neurotip, 128 Hz tuning fork and cotton wool. Examine in this order: inspection, gait, tone, power, reflexes, coordination, sensation. Inspect for distress, habitus, abnormal movements, deformity, aids and equipment such as a catheter, then for wasting, fasciculations, scars and skin changes. Assess gait (walk, turn and walk back; heel-to-toe; heels; toes), staying close to prevent falls, then Romberg's test, squat and Trendelenburg, and mention the pull test. Test tone and clonus at the knee and ankle. Grade power on the MRC scale. Test knee, ankle and plantar reflexes and describe them correctly (absent, reduced, normal, brisk). Test heel-shin, toe-finger and foot tapping. Test sensation with eyes closed, by dermatome, comparing sides and against a normal area such as the sternum. Test at least one spinothalamic modality (pinprick, temperature) and one dorsal column modality (vibration, proprioception); light touch travels in both. If sensation is abnormal throughout the legs, keep going up the trunk to find a level. Complete with the upper limbs, cranial nerves, a lower limb musculoskeletal examination and anal tone.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: every value is in the white zone, but the sensory level rises from T10 to T8 and the nurse is concerned. A spinal cord lesion worsens neurologically, not on the vital signs. Under Between the Flags, staff concern is itself a Clinical Review criterion. A rising level needs immediate review and attention to the arms, cough and breathing. The T8 level is now above the lesion imaged at 11:00 (at about the T10-T11 cord segments), so the inflammation has extended or swollen since the scan; it is still below T6 and spares the diaphragm, but lower intercostal and abdominal weakness can weaken her cough.
  • Bloods: normal inflammatory markers and an afebrile patient make an epidural abscess unlikely. Normal coagulation makes a haematoma unlikely and the LP safe. A normal B12 and a negative β-hCG (confirming the triage urine test done before gadolinium) complete the baseline; glucose is the baseline for steroid monitoring.
  • MRI: the key question is whether anything compresses the cord, because that decides neurosurgery or neurology. Whole-spine imaging is needed because the clinical level can sit below the true lesion and there may be more than one lesion. Vertebral and cord levels differ: in the lower thoracic spine a cord segment lies about three vertebrae above its number, and the sensory level is at or below the lesion, never above it. Lesion shape helps separate the causes: MS cord lesions are short, peripheral (often dorsolateral) and occupy less than half the cross-section; NMOSD lesions are usually long (3 or more segments) and central.

Management

  • Emergency first: a new spastic paraparesis with a sensory level and sphincter involvement is a neurosurgical emergency until proven otherwise. It needs urgent senior review and an urgent MRI of the whole spine. If MRI shows compression, call neurosurgery at once (with dexamethasone for malignant compression and antibiotics for an abscess, per the relevant eTG guidance).
  • Demyelinating myelitis (eTG Neurology; specialist-led): once compression and infection are excluded, high-dose methylprednisolone, typically 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days, speeds recovery from an acute relapse. Plasma exchange is considered for severe attacks that do not respond to steroids. Monitor glucose and mood on steroids.
  • Work-up: lumbar puncture (cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands with a paired serum sample, and infection testing), ideally before the first methylprednisolone dose if this does not delay treatment, and serum aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies. Neurology decides on long-term disease-modifying therapy.
  • Supportive care: catheter care and bladder management; a bowel regimen; VTE prophylaxis after risk assessment (she is immobile and on the combined pill), timed around the LP; withhold the combined pill while she is immobile and advise alternative contraception, which also matters if a disease-modifying therapy that needs contraception is started; pressure area care; falls precautions; early physiotherapy and occupational therapy.
  • Disposition: admit under neurology, with neurological observations of the level, power, arms and breathing.

Safety netting and follow-up

On the ward, nurses escalate a rising sensory level, weakness or numbness spreading to the arms, breathing difficulty or a weak cough, new fever or severe back pain, and catheter problems. Before discharge, Katie needs to know in plain words to call 000 for rapidly spreading weakness or trouble breathing. New visual loss, or weakness, numbness or bladder symptoms lasting more than a day, are possible relapses that need prompt review by neurology or the ED. Follow-up is with the neurology clinic and an MS nurse, rehabilitation, and her GP. She should not drive until neurology has assessed her fitness under the Austroads standards. She will also need a work certificate.
points: Decide upper or lower motor neuron first, then localise. Spastic tone, brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars mean an upper motor neuron lesion; normal arms with a truncal sensory level put it in the thoracic cord.

When sensation is abnormal throughout both legs, keep testing up the trunk to find a sensory level (T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal ligament), and always ask about bladder, bowel and perianal sensation.
A new paraparesis with a sensory level and sphincter involvement is cord compression until proven otherwise. Escalate to a senior and get an urgent MRI of the whole spine.
Cauda equina syndrome gives lower motor neuron signs and saddle anaesthesia. Upper motor neuron signs with a truncal level mean the problem is in the cord.

A short, peripheral, enhancing myelitis with periventricular and juxtacortical brain lesions, after a past optic neuritis, is a second demyelinating attack and points to multiple sclerosis. Neurology treats it with high-dose methylprednisolone and confirms it with CSF and antibody testing (AQP4, MOG).
A spinal cord lesion worsens on the neurological examination, not the vital signs. A rising sensory level or new arm weakness needs immediate review, even when the chart is in the white zone.
